sources.title: Evacuation and Internment

sources.annotation: Illustrated account of U.S. removal, inadequate Southeast Alaska camps and evacuees' work rebuilding daily life. Includes attributed survivor excerpts. Read it alongside the commission report for the different rationales of wartime evacuation and prolonged confinement.

sources.title: Unangax̂ Restitution
sources.author: National Park Service; survivor perspectives excerpted from Aleut Story
sources.annotation: Explains survivors' testimony, advocacy and the limits of financial redress, with excerpts attributed to Flore Lekanof and Alice Snigaroff Petrivelli. Its legal summary should be checked against the original statute.

sources.title: Public Law 100–383: §2(b) and Title II, Aleutian and Pribilof Islands Restitution Act
sources.publisher: United States Congress; Statutes at Large via GovInfo
sources.author: United States Congress
sources.annotation: Original law enacted August 10, 1988. Distinguishes congressional findings, defined individual eligibility, community-loss compensation and Attu land restitution. This historical enactment is more precise than a general account of compensation.

sources.title: Personal Justice Denied, Part II: The Aleuts — War and Evacuation in Alaska
sources.publisher: Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians; National Archives full-text copy
sources.author: Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians
sources.annotation: Official 1982 investigation distinguishes evacuation under attack from failures of planning, camp administration and return. Selected opening and concluding pages inspected, rather than the entire report. Read its dated cultural-loss framing alongside contemporary community accounts.

sources.title: Attu Boy
sources.publisher: National Park Service, Aleutian World War II National Historic Area, in cooperation with the Aleutian Pribilof Heritage Group
sources.author: Nick Golodoff; Rachel Mason, editor; Brenda Maly, preface and transcription
sources.annotation: Golodoff's childhood recollections are presented with other Attuan accounts and Mason's commentary. Maly explains the uncertainties of early memory. Selected passages on captivity and resettlement provide a personal perspective without treating one narrator as every survivor.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: U.S. removal and survival in Southeast Alaska
claimBlocks.text: After the 1942 attacks, U.S. authorities removed villagers to Southeast Alaska. The NPS account documents makeshift camp buildings, unsafe water, inadequate care and deadly illness. It also describes evacuees finding work, repairing housing and establishing community facilities. These actions belong in the account alongside government neglect: displaced families continued organizing daily life under conditions they had not chosen.

Survivors and community members pressed for recognition by recounting traumatic experiences, documenting losses and taking their case to Washington. The NPS restitution account presents this as sustained Unangax̂ organizing. Its survivor perspectives also show why acknowledgment and funds could assist rebuilding without replacing lost relatives, homes or cultural belongings.

Public Law 100–383 acknowledged U.S. failures of care and property protection. Title II separated community losses from individual compensation for specifically defined eligible persons, and addressed Attu lands through compensation in lieu of conveyance. These were distinct historical remedies; they should not be described as identical payments to every Unangax̂ person or as restoration of Attu village.

The 1982 commission distinguished the Aleut evacuation from Japanese American exclusion: it considered removal from islands under attack a reasonable safety precaution. It nevertheless documented failures to plan, deplorable camps, looted homes and delayed return. Keeping those findings together explains how an evacuation prompted by a real attack became a history of preventable official harm.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Attu captivity and the limits of return
claimBlocks.text: Attu residents faced a separate ordeal: Japanese forces took them to Japan. In Attu Boy, Nick Golodoff recalls confinement, hunger and illness through a child's memories; his granddaughter and editor make their uncertainties visible. His return account describes being sent to Atka, where relatives provided housing. Survival and release therefore did not mean restoration of his former home on Attu.
